title: asyncio and asynchronous I/O

spans.text: WHY USE THIS?
asyncio schedules I/O-waiting tasks on an event loop, usually in one thread.
async def
defines a coroutine and
await
yields control;
gather

returns results in input order, while a Semaphore bounds concurrent work. Blocking I/O and CPU-heavy code stall the loop. Design timeouts, cancellation, and task lifetimes; use a process pool or suitable executor for CPU parallelism.
CORE EXPLANATION
asyncio coordinates I/O-heavy tasks on an event loop. async def defines a coroutine, and await yields while it waits for completion.
EXAMPLE CODE
QUESTION: What will this code print? Predict first, then run it.

spans.code:
import asyncio

async def read_sensor(name: str, gate: asyncio.Semaphore) -> str:
    async with gate:
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return f'{name}:ready'

async def main() -> None:
    gate = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        read_sensor('temperature', gate),
        read_sensor('humidity', gate),
    )
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

spans.title: Important tip
spans.text: Async does not automatically parallelize CPU-heavy computation.

spans.title: Warning
spans.text: Concurrency must respect service limits and local resource bounds.

    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.sleep(1), timeout=0.01)
    except TimeoutError:
        print('operation timed out')

asyncio.run(main())

spans.title: Why it matters
spans.text: asyncio schedules I/O-waiting tasks on an event loop, usually in one thread. `async def` defines a coroutine and `await` yields control; `gather` returns results in input order, while a Semaphore bounds concurrent work. Blocking I/O and CPU-heavy code stall the loop. Design timeouts, cancellation, and task lifetimes; use a process pool or suitable executor for CPU parallelism.
COMMON MISTAKES
Avoid blocking I/O inside an async endpoint; use an async-compatible client.
